title: Range Queries and Ladders
focus: The two hardest structures you are actually expected to write, and BFS over an implicit word graph.

cards.title: Trapping Rain Water
patterns: Water is bounded by the smaller max
cards.trigger: Each position's answer depends on the maximum to its left and the maximum to its right.
cards.recall: Write the two-pointer version from memory. Then answer the argument that makes it correct: when `left_max < right_max`, why is it safe to finalise the left column without ever looking at the right side again?
useWhen: Trapping rain water, 1D and 2D
Container with most water, a simpler cousin
Any per-index bounded-by-both-sides quantity
Skyline-ish coverage questions
Where a prefix-max and suffix-max pair would work but you want O(1) space
template: # left_max is the true bound here: right side is guaranteed taller
# Easier to explain, O(n) space: precompute prefix max and suffix max,
# 2D version is a min-heap starting from the whole border, always
# expanding from the lowest boundary cell inward.
keyInsights: Water above a column is min(left_max, right_max) minus its height. Everything else is how to know that minimum cheaply
Moving the smaller side is what guarantees the side you finalise is the binding constraint
If you cannot explain the two-pointer version, write the prefix and suffix version. A correct O(n) space answer beats a shaky O(1) one
cards.trap: 'Now it is a 2D elevation map.' Two pointers do not generalise. It becomes a min-heap flood from the border inwards, and that is a genuinely different algorithm.

cards.title: Segment Tree

Range maximum with updates, where a BIT will not do
Count of elements in a value range, over a compressed axis
Range assign or range add, with lazy propagation
Any associative combine over ranges

complexity.time: O(n) build, O(log n) update and query

keyInsights: The combine must be associative. Sum, min, max and gcd qualify. Median and mode do not
For plain prefix sums a Fenwick tree is half the code. Reach for a segment tree when the aggregate is min, max, or needs lazy range updates

cards.trap: 'Range updates, not just point updates.' You need lazy propagation, which is a real amount of extra machinery. Say so rather than trying to bolt it on live.

problem.name: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree

keyInsights: The sort by value on ties is what makes this a hard problem instead of a medium one. BFS order alone gives the wrong answer
Tracking min and max column while traversing lets you skip the sort of the keys, dropping to O(n) for the column ordering
Top and bottom view are the same traversal with a different reduce over each column bucket
cards.trap: 'Is BFS order enough for ties?' No, and that is precisely the difference between this problem and its easier lookalike. Read the tie-break rule before coding.

cards.title: Bitmask DP
cards.trigger: A small set of items, and the state you need is 'which subset have I already used'.
cards.recall: Write the k-equal-subsets solver from memory. Then answer the sizing question: what makes bitmask DP viable, and at what n does it stop being viable?
useWhen: Partition into k equal-sum subsets
Minimum sessions or minimum groups to finish tasks
Travelling salesman on a small graph
Shortest path visiting all nodes
Any assignment problem with n at most about 20
template: nums.sort(reverse=True)            # big items first prunes hard

problem.name: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets

keyInsights: The mask alone is enough state because the running sum is derivable from it, which is why memoising on mask works
2^20 is about a million, which is fine. 2^25 is 33 million and marginal. 2^30 is not happening
Sorting descending makes the impossible branches fail early, and on this problem that is the difference between passing and timing out
cards.trap: 'n is 40.' Bitmask is dead. Meet in the middle, split into two halves of 20 and combine, is the intended answer. Know the name.

cards.title: Implicit Graph BFS
patterns: Nodes are states, edges are computed
cards.trigger: Shortest transformation between two states, where the graph is never materialised.
cards.recall: Write word ladder from memory. Then answer the efficiency question: generating neighbours by trying 26 letters at each position is O(26 * L). What is the preprocessing that makes it O(L)?
useWhen: Word ladder, minimum genetic mutation
Open the lock, minimum turns
Sliding puzzle, board states as nodes
Minimum operations to reach a number
Any shortest sequence of moves between states
template: if end not in words: return 0
# Preprocess: 'h*t' -> ['hot', 'hit', ...] so neighbours are a dict lookup
# Bidirectional BFS: grow from both ends, always expand the smaller frontier.
keyInsights: The graph is never built. Neighbours are computed on demand, which is what 'implicit graph' means
Wildcard bucketing turns neighbour generation into a dictionary lookup and is the standard optimisation here
Bidirectional BFS roughly square-roots the search space. Mention it even if you write the one-directional version
cards.trap: 'Return every shortest path, not just the length.' You must record predecessors per level and backtrack afterwards. Substantially harder, and a very common follow-up.
